hints: Check each option by matching the vessel to the chamber it actually connects to, does the aorta really leave the right side and does the vena cava really enter the right side?
Remember the two valve rules: atria fill passively when relaxed, and blood only leaves ventricles through semilunar valves while it only enters ventricles through atrioventricular valves.
walkthrough:
**Map the plumbing first**

Think of the heart as two separate pumps side by side. The right side handles deoxygenated blood: vena cava into right atrium into right ventricle into pulmonary artery. The left side handles oxygenated blood: pulmonary vein into left atrium into left ventricle into aorta.

**Apply the valve and pressure rule**

Blood always flows from high pressure to low pressure. When an atrium relaxes (atrial diastole), its pressure falls so blood is drawn in from its vein. When a ventricle contracts (ventricular systole), its pressure rises so blood is pushed out through the semilunar valve. Blood from atrium to ventricle always passes through an atrioventricular valve, never a semilunar valve.

**Pick the only matching statement**

Only option C fits both the vessel map and the valve rule: vena cava to right atrium during relaxation. All the others mix up right with left, artery with vein, or AV valve with semilunar valve.

options.A: Incorrect, the aorta leaves the left ventricle, not the right. Contraction of the right ventricle pushes blood into the pulmonary artery.
options.B: Incorrect, the left atrium receives blood through the pulmonary vein, not the pulmonary artery. The pulmonary artery carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs.
options.C: Correct, when the right atrial wall relaxes its pressure drops, so deoxygenated blood flows in from the vena cava. This is normal atrial filling in diastole.
options.D: Incorrect, blood enters the right ventricle from the right atrium through the tricuspid atrioventricular valve, not a semilunar valve. Semilunar valves only guard the exits from the ventricles.
